chapter: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
title: Lindy Hop, carnival dancers and ballyhoo
summary: Dancers and horn players in carnivals spread new dances; Smith played ballyhoo on trucks in Oklahoma and for shows in Dallas.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: When you'd play this more rhythmic music for the Black dancers, were they doing sort of the Lindy and things like that, even in the country places?
What do you mean?
Buster Smith - 124
You don't remember the Lindy Hop and the Jitterbug.
Yeah! Oh yes.
Were they doing that kind of stuff?
Yeah.
Even in the country areas.

Yeah, sure. Heh-heh. Yeah, they'd come to town and see (?)our dates(?) and all that kind of thing, and see the... I'll tell you, a lot of the.(?) carried a lot of that theatrical stuff around the country with them, was spreading around, advertising... You know who did it? Carnivals.
Oh really.
Yeah. They had guys working on the carnivals there, and standing on them stands up there...
Dancers.

Yeah. Dancers and the horn players. They'd have two or three horns and drums, and all (?) that. Then they'd come, and them guys would see them dancing and going to hear that new dance, and everybody would pick right up on it.
Is this what they used to call the ballyhoo? They'd do a ballyhoo?

No. A ballyhoo is mostly for what these show things where they have the... Well, sometimes we used to play ballyhoo up there in Oklahoma, get on a truck, and then be sitting on that and drive all up and down the street.
Buster Smith - 125
To advertise?

Yeah. Advertising the dance hall. We did that two or three times. But most of the time, whenever you'd see these gals(?) and things, that's the one that brings on the ballyhoo. Because a man got a' good ...(?)... at a bunch of girls back in them days, and he couldn't (?), and then when you'd go out there and ballyhoo about 30 minutes out in front, all the people roll up and down to attract the people, and the man's out there with a big mike, talkin', "Come on in! There's a show goin' on in a few minutes!" and all of that. Then the people come pilin' in there. We have to play the show, and then got to go right back out there and ballyhoo. We had to do that, start 11 o'clock in the morning until 12 o'clock at night, and never stopped. Never stopped playing. Yeah, right here in Dallas.
So I'm not quite clear. This carnival thing you're talking about, where they advertised new dances, that wasn't to bring the people into the carnival. It was just part of the carnival.
Yeah. Mmm-hmm.
Like one of the acts in the carnival.

Yeah. But you mean the guy... You had them little small carnivals. Well, that man advertising, he'd draw the folks up there, then the minute they'd get the people in there and they'd stop the band and stop ...(?)..., and let them go out through the crowd selling medicine. Yes, selling some kind of
Buster Smith - 126
patent medicine he got. That's how he made his money.
And when they put on this couple doing the latest dance, or whatever it is, would that be to attract people into the carnival?
Uh-huh. Yeah.
Or would it be once they'd got inside?
Yeah, it would be just to attract the people, to get them to come on inside.
So it was rather like a ballyhoo.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
[PAUSE]
